## What it computes

The three-valued answer to whether $x = y$ for every $x \in X, y \in Y$, $X$ and $Y$ not being empty, $X = [x_l, x_u]$ and $Y = [y_l, y_u]$: *yes* only if it holds for every choice of members, *no* only if it fails for every choice, otherwise *unknown*, both masks false:

$$\mathit{yes} \implies X \ne \emptyset, Y \ne \emptyset \text{ and } x = y \text{ for every } x \in X, y \in Y, \qquad \mathit{no} \implies X \ne \emptyset, Y \ne \emptyset \text{ and } \lnot(x = y) \text{ for every } x \in X, y \in Y.$$

## C++

**Not yet called by the public headers.** No public operation computes this kernel yet.

## Requires

- $X = [x_l, x_u]$ is a canonical interval: the empty set, $x_l = +\infty$ and $x_u = -\infty$, or a nonempty interval, neither bound a NaN, $x_l \le x_u$, $x_l < +\infty$, $x_u > -\infty$, each bound a number of `T` or an infinity; its members are the real numbers between its bounds.
- $Y = [y_l, y_u]$ is a canonical interval: the empty set, $y_l = +\infty$ and $y_u = -\infty$, or a nonempty interval, neither bound a NaN, $y_l \le y_u$, $y_l < +\infty$, $y_u > -\infty$, each bound a number of `T` or an infinity; its members are the real numbers between its bounds.

## Target (not proved)

For operands that satisfy the requirements, finite, infinite or NaN:

- $\mathit{yes}$ is true only if $X \ne \emptyset, Y \ne \emptyset \text{ and } x = y \text{ for every } x \in X, y \in Y$; $\mathit{no}$ only if $X \ne \emptyset, Y \ne \emptyset \text{ and } \lnot(x = y) \text{ for every } x \in X, y \in Y$; never both. Both false is the answer *unknown*.
- An empty operand gives *unknown*, and so does the whole line.
- Exact: $\mathit{yes}$ is true exactly when $X \ne \emptyset, Y \ne \emptyset \text{ and } x = y \text{ for every } x \in X, y \in Y$, and $\mathit{no}$ exactly when $X \ne \emptyset, Y \ne \emptyset \text{ and } \lnot(x = y) \text{ for every } x \in X, y \in Y$; *unknown* is returned exactly when neither holds.

Stated for every binary format with a precision of at least 1 bit, rounding to nearest with ties to even and with gradual underflow, in the IEEE model, with signed zeros, infinities, NaN and overflow. Both limb types qualify: `double` has 53 bits, `float` has 24 bits.

## Source

**Algorithm:** the bounds compared, and a test of emptiness (Milestone 2 listing). **License:** algorithm and proof: MIT.

## Listing

From [`gen/kernels/interval_equal_1.kernel`](https://github.com/danielepanozzo/kairn/blob/main/gen/kernels/interval_equal_1.kernel), the description the C++ and the formal model (`proofs/gen/IeeeModel.v`) are generated from. Each line is one operation of `T`; one that rounds rounds to nearest, and `prod(a, b)` is $\mathrm{RN}(ab)$, written as a fused multiply-add with a zero addend ([the kernel IR](../developer/architecture.md#the-kernel-ir)).

```
# The three-valued X = Y of intervals with one-limb bounds (milestone2.md, "One enclosure
# interface", "Comparisons"): yes when every member of X equals every member of Y, that is X = Y =
# [v, v], x_l = x_u = y_l = y_u; no when no member of X equals one of Y, the intervals disjoint, x_u
# < y_l or y_u < x_l; both false otherwise and when an operand is empty (the yes of the empty set
# fails by itself: its bounds differ). By the comparisons of T. Exact. For every precision.

ea  = eq(xl, xu)
eb  = eq(xu, yl)
ec  = eq(yl, yu)
eab = and(ea, eb)
yes = and(eab, ec)
nx  = lt(xl, const inf)
ny  = lt(yl, const inf)
ne  = and(nx, ny)
da  = lt(xu, yl)
db  = lt(yu, xl)
dd  = or(da, db)
no  = and(dd, ne)
```
